title: KNICKS EXTENSION BOMBSHELL! Towns and Hart Are STAYING… But the Writing Is on the Wall for McBride
thumb_prompt: an empty locker in a dim Madison Square Garden tunnel with a jersey missing from the hook and a countdown clock glowing behind it
thumb_subject: a young guard in a blue and orange jersey looking away from camera

paragraphs.text: A well connected Knicks insider just dropped a massive update on the contract extension situations for three key members of this championship roster. Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, and Miles McBride. And there is a lot to unpack here, because these three stories are heading in very different directions. One of them is going to sting for a lot of you watching this.
We are breaking down every single one of these latest reports today, piece by piece, so you know exactly where this roster stands heading into the season.

Hey, what is going on everybody, welcome back to the channel. Before we jump into all of this, do me one quick favor. Smash that like button right now while you are thinking about it. It takes you literally one second, but it tells YouTube to push this video out to more Knicks fans just like you. And if you are new here and you love daily Knicks coverage, hit subscribe and ring the bell. Alright, let us get into it.

sections.heading: THE UPDATE EVERYBODY WAS WAITING FOR

paragraphs.text: So here is the situation. We have all been refreshing our feeds waiting for the same piece of news. Have the Knicks officially extended Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, or Miles McBride yet? The short answer is no. None of those deals have been signed as of right now.

But do not click away, because we have meaningful updates on all three of these situations. And when you line them up side by side, a very clear picture starts to form about where this front office is heading.
card_lines: Line them up side by side

paragraphs.text: Let us start with the big one. Karl-Anthony Towns. We all know KAT is going to get a contract extension from the Knicks at some point. That part is not really in question. The real question, the one worth millions and millions of dollars, is for how much.

Thanks to NBA insider Ian Begley of SNY, we actually have some clarity on that now. According to him, Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart and Miles McBride are all currently eligible for veteran extensions. So the door is open for all three. The money, though, is where things get complicated.

Here is where it gets interesting. James Edwards the third, an NBA insider over at The Athletic who covers this team as closely as anybody, said he does not expect the Knicks to put a max contract on the table for Towns.

Now before anybody gets upset, let us be clear about something. Towns is a Knick for life in the hearts of this fanbase. What he did during New York's championship season is going to be celebrated for as long as this franchise exists. Decades from now, people are going to be telling their kids about that run. That is locked in forever, no matter what happens with this contract.

But I have got to be honest with you. I agree with Edwards on this one. I do not see the Knicks offering Towns a max in these extension talks. And if I had to put money on it, I still believe the two sides find common ground and get a deal done. Why? Because Towns clearly loves New York. You can see it every time he talks about this city, this fanbase, this organization. This is his hometown team, and he won a ring wearing that jersey.

Could he theoretically chase more money with another team next summer? Sure, that option technically exists. Towns is pulling in a fifty seven million dollar salary this season, and his current deal includes a sixty one million dollar player option for the 2027-28 season. Those are enormous numbers. But even Ian Begley believes Karl-Anthony Towns is going to earn less on his next contract with the Knicks than what a max would pay him.

So the natural follow up question is, what number does KAT actually say yes to? Begley gives us a pretty strong hint. According to his reporting, if you use the recent Rudy Gobert extension as a baseline, and that is a very reasonable comparison for a star big man at this stage, you could see an extension for Towns starting somewhere around forty five million per year.

Now let us talk about what that actually means. By signing a deal in that range, Towns would be giving up the chance to chase bigger money as a free agent in 2027. That is a real sacrifice, and nobody should pretend otherwise.

But when you zoom out and look at all the factors in play, the current state of NBA economics, the way teams around the league are treating that second apron like it is radioactive, and the fact that the Knicks just won a title, there are very legitimate reasons for Towns to play it safe and lock in that security now. A bird in the hand, as they say.

And flip it around for a second, because this cuts both ways. Towns walking out of New York would hurt the Knicks badly. If KAT and the front office cannot come to terms, this team would suddenly have to make a massive pivot just to find another frontline center. And if you have been following the backup center saga this offseason, you know exactly how thin that market is.

So from the outside looking in, this feels like a situation where both sides need each other, and both sides know it. And Begley basically confirms that read. In his view, KAT does not really have a compelling reason to leave. Why would he? He won a championship with his hometown team, in the biggest market in basketball. Unless the Knicks come in with some insultingly low offer, and I do not believe for a second that they will, I think this gets done.

Quick pause. If you are getting value out of this breakdown, hit that subscribe button if you have not already. It is free, it takes half a second, and it means the algorithm actually shows you the next video instead of burying it. Alright, back to business.

So what about Josh Hart and his extension? Is he taking a discount too? According to Ian Begley, yeah, he could see that happening as well. His exact read is that, similar to Towns, the Knicks are likely going to ask Hart to take less on his next contract, all in the name of creating future roster flexibility.
card_lines: Same ask from the front office

paragraphs.text: What does Hart himself want to do? Honestly, nobody outside his inner circle knows for sure. But if I had to guess, and Begley leans this way too, Hart wants to be in New York. He wants to see how the rest of this core's championship window plays out. He is a culture guy, he is a glue guy, he bleeds for this team every single night, and guys like that do not usually walk away from a title contender at the peak of its powers.

So the picture forming here is that both Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart are likely taking less on their next deals, but both of them are staying. That is the trade-off, and frankly, it is the kind of trade-off championship organizations are built on.

sections.heading: THE WRINKLE NOBODY IS TALKING ABOUT

paragraphs.text: Now here is where it gets really interesting, because there is a wrinkle in all of this that a lot of people are completely sleeping on. Stefan Bondy, NBA insider with the New York Post, dropped this piece of information, and pay close attention because this matters.
card_lines: Bondy of the New York Post

paragraphs.text: According to Bondy, Josh Hart and Karl-Anthony Towns are in a different boat than most extension candidates, because the numbers they are expected to sign at will not necessarily wipe out their trade eligibility.

Let me explain the mechanics, because this is genuinely important. Under league rules, a player who signs a veteran extension cannot be traded for six months if his new deal includes a first year raise of more than twenty percent, includes annual raises greater than five percent, or runs for at least four years. Those are the triggers.

But here is the thing. The Knicks want both of these guys to take less. And if the deals come in modest enough to stay under those thresholds, the ability to trade them remains fully intact. Now, I am not saying the Knicks are planning to trade Towns or Hart. Put the pitchforks down. What I am saying is this front office is building in maximum flexibility at every single turn, and that is exactly what a smart championship organization does. Every door stays open.

And then there is Miles McBride. Deuce. And folks, his situation is nothing like the other two. Unlike Towns and Hart, McBride is in line for a significant raise from the roughly four million dollar salary he is playing on this season.

According to Ian Begley once again, McBride's situation is fundamentally different because of where his contract sits. The man is on one of the most team friendly deals in the entire NBA, genuinely one of the best value contracts in basketball, and he should absolutely be looking for a major raise on any extension. He has earned every penny of it.

But here is the brutal math problem. Can the Knicks realistically extend Towns, Hart and McBride while still maintaining some roster flexibility? If they intend to stay under that second apron, and we will get to why that is non-negotiable in a minute, the answer is probably no. It would be extraordinarily difficult to build out a functional roster with all three of those new extensions sitting on the books.

And do not forget the elephant in the room. The Knicks presumably still have to hand Jalen Brunson a major extension or free agency contract when his time comes. That money has to be accounted for. And remember, Brunson is the guy who set the precedent for a Knicks star taking less on an extension specifically to help build out this roster. That sacrifice is a huge part of why there is a banner hanging in the Garden right now.

So when you add it all up, it looks like New York simply will not be able to extend all three players. Towns and Hart take less, get extended, and stay. And Miles McBride? He is looking like the odd man out.

sections.heading: THE WRITING IS ON THE WALL

paragraphs.text: And if you needed more evidence, take a look at this update from Stefan Bondy about McBride, his extension, and the very real possibility of him being moved. According to Bondy, this does not mean a Deuce McBride extension can never happen down the road, but yesterday was something of a soft deadline, and it came and went with no agreement between the Knicks and McBride's camp.

Here is why that date mattered so much. If McBride signs an extension now, he becomes ineligible to be traded before the February trade deadline. Read that again. The Knicks deliberately let a deadline pass that would have locked McBride onto the roster through February. By missing it, they preserved the ability to trade him at the deadline.

Ladies and gentlemen, the writing is on the wall. New York is likely not extending Miles McBride. And if they are not extending him, the next logical step is that he gets traded. Either before the season tips off, or at some point before that February deadline. It hurts to say about a homegrown champion, but the breadcrumbs all point in the same direction.
paragraphs.card_title: THE WRITING IS ON THE WALL

paragraphs.text: If you are a Deuce believer, I know this one stings. Drop your reaction in the comments below, because I have watched this fanbase go to absolute war over this guy and I want to hear where you stand. Extend him anyway? Trade him for frontcourt help? Let me know. I read every single comment.

Now, some of you are sitting there asking the obvious question. Why can New York not just extend all three guys? It is the biggest market in the league. The money exists. What is the holdup? The main answer comes down to James Dolan and that dreaded second apron.

The owner still does not want this team crossing into second apron territory, and honestly, the penalties for doing so are genuinely punishing. Frozen draft picks, restricted trade mechanics, no aggregating salaries, the works. It is designed to be painful, and it is.

According to Ian Begley once more, another major element of this conversation is Dolan's stance on spending. Dolan went on WFAN before free agency and stated flat out that he would not exceed the second apron in team salary next season. Now, the open questions are, does that stance extend to 2027-28? What about 2028-29? Nobody knows for certain yet, and that uncertainty hangs over every one of these negotiations.

As a side note, it is genuinely unclear whether the second apron decision was Dolan's call alone or something decided together with Leon Rose and the front office. If it was purely Dolan acting solo, that would be a shame, because this fanbase spends serious money to pack that building every single night, and they deserve an ownership group willing to go all in on a title window. That said, Dolan and Rose have made plenty of major decisions jointly throughout Rose's tenure, so the truth is probably somewhere in the middle.

sections.heading: WHERE I LAND ON ALL OF THIS

paragraphs.text: Look, I will be straight with you about where I stand. I wanted everybody back. I wanted New York to extend every player they possibly could and run this exact championship group back into the ground.

But as I said weeks ago on this channel, that dream was always unlikely. And given everything we just walked through, it is now painfully obvious. Towns and Hart take less and stay. McBride likely gets moved, either before opening night or at the deadline. That is the reality.
